patterns.target: Word order in an embedded question
patterns.why: An embedded question keeps statement word order — {ans} — because the auxiliary of a direct question belongs only to a direct question.
A yes/no question embedded inside a statement is introduced by whether or if and keeps statement word order: {ans}.
After a past reporting verb such as said, will backshifts to would: {ans}.
This verb takes an infinitive rather than a gerund: {ans}.
This verb takes a gerund rather than an infinitive: {ans}.
A preposition must be followed by a gerund, never an infinitive: {ans}.
A situation that began in the past and still continues takes the present perfect: {ans}.

patterns.target: Past perfect for the earlier past event
patterns.why: When one past event precedes another, the earlier one takes the past perfect: {ans}.
An unreal conditional uses a past form in the if clause and would or could plus a base verb in the other: {ans}.
A past unreal conditional pairs had plus a past participle with would have plus a past participle: {ans}.
A likely future condition takes a present form after if and will in the main clause: {ans}.
The passive is a form of be plus a past participle: {ans}. Been appears only after have or had.
After a modal the passive keeps be plus a past participle: {ans}.
Who introduces a clause describing a person and acts as its subject, so no second subject pronoun follows: {ans}.
Whose shows possession and attaches directly to the noun it owns: {ans}. Who cannot be followed by a noun this way.
A relative clause can drop its pronoun and verb, leaving a participle that modifies the noun directly: {ans}.
A comparative form is completed by than, never by as: {ans}.
An equal comparison brackets the adjective or adverb between two instances of as: {ans}.
A superlative takes the and compares one thing against a whole group: {ans}.
The the … the … pattern puts the comparative phrase first in each half and follows each with a clause: {ans}.

patterns.target: Separable phrasal verb with a pronoun object
patterns.why: When the object of a separable phrasal verb is a pronoun it must come between the verb and the particle: {ans}.
When a negative or limiting adverbial opens a sentence, the subject and auxiliary invert: {ans}.
So goes with an adjective or adverb and such with a noun phrase; either is completed by a that clause: {ans}.
Too comes before an adjective and enough comes after it: {ans}.
A causative puts the object before the past participle, because someone else does the work: {ans}.
Make and let take an object followed by a bare infinitive, with no to: {ans}.
Used to plus a base verb names a discontinued past habit, while be used to plus a gerund or noun means accustomed to something: {ans}.
A wish about the present takes a past form, and were for every subject: {ans}.
A regret about the past takes wish plus the past perfect: {ans}.
Both had better and would rather are followed by a bare infinitive, with no to: {ans}.

patterns.target: Modal of deduction about the past
patterns.why: A deduction about the past takes a modal plus have plus a past participle: {ans}.
A question folded inside a polite request keeps statement word order after the question word: {ans}.

patterns.target: Quantifiers with count and noncount nouns
patterns.why: Countable nouns take few, many and number; uncountable nouns take little, much and amount: {ans}.
The verb agrees with the head of the subject, not with a noun that happens to sit next to it: {ans}.
Having plus a past participle compresses a completed earlier action into a clause with no subject of its own: {ans}.
Correlative pairs such as not only … but also, both … and and either … or must join two grammatically parallel elements: {ans}.
A frequency adverb goes before a main verb, but after be and after the first auxiliary: {ans}.
Will have plus a past participle looks back from a future point; will be plus an -ing form describes something in progress then: {ans}.
Although and even though introduce a clause, while despite and in spite of introduce a noun phrase or gerund: {ans}.
Purpose is expressed by so that plus a clause or in order to plus a base verb: {ans}.
